## Large R01 2024

aim1_power.Rmd - This was the MWAS (ssizeRNA R package, Bi, R. & Liu, P. ssizeRNA: Sample Size Calculation for RNA-Seq Experimental Design. (2019).)
```{r}
#| label: pfas_pesticides_R01

# Categorical
check.power(m = 2322, # sample size per treatment group
            nGenes = 707, # total number of genes, here exposomics chemicals
            mu = 1e4, # mean counts in control group
            pi0 = 0.90, # proportion of non-differentially expressed genes
            disp = 0.5, # dispersion parameter
            fc = 1.1, # fold change
            sims = 1, # number of simulations
            fdr = 0.05) # false discovery rate

# Continuous????
check.power(m = 13000, # sample size per treatment group
            nGenes = 707, # total number of genes, here exposomics chemicals
            mu = 1e4, # mean counts in control group
            pi0 = 0.90, # proportion of non-differentially expressed genes
            disp = 0.5, # dispersion parameter
            fc = 1.1, # fold change
            sims = 1, # number of simulations
            fdr = 0.05) # false discovery rate

```

power = 92.0%, power unchanged for single metabolite models
Note: m comes from 2322 Dementia or CIND cases, like Aim 1 above
Power text: For untargeted differential abundance metabolomics analysis, assuming that 10% of 707 detected
metabolites are differentially abundant with an average abundance of 10,000 and dispersion of 0.5 among
2,322 individuals with incident CIND or dementia, we have 92.0% power to detect a log-fold-change of 1.1, (q-value false
discovery rate=0.05). (CITATION) 


Aim 2 (ERS) mixtures power
```{r}
#| label: ers_mixtures_R01
#| 
# Exponentiate for the logistic regression
exp(0.07)

# For the cox regression
powerEpiCont.default(n = 13000, # total number of subjects
                     theta = 1.09, # postulated HR
                     sigma2 = 1, # variance of the covariate of interest
                     psi = 0.172, # proportion of subjects with the disease
                     rho2 = 0.2, # square of the multiple correlation coefficient between covariate of interest and other covariates
                     alpha=0.05)
```

Linear multiple regression, GPower (details below), power = 98.0%

Test family: F tests
Statistical test: Linear multiple regression: fixed model, R2 deviation from zero
Type of power analysis: Post hoc: compute achieved power - given alpha, sample size, and effect size
Input parameters: 
Effect size f2: 0.001 --> 0.002 -->  0.01
Alpha: 0.05
Total sample size: 13000
Number of predictors: 7
Power: 75.1% --> 98.0% --> 100%

Logistic regression, GPower (details below), power = 98.7%, note that this is assuming prevalence of CIND or dementia outcome with 17.2% prevalence of outcome

Test family: Exact
Statistical test: Linear multiple regression: Random model
Type of power analysis: Post hoc: compute achieved power - given alpha, sample size, and effect size
Input parameters:
Tails: two
H1 p2: 0.3 --> 0.07
H0 p2: 0
alpha: 0.05
Total sample size: 4472 (1300*0.172*2)
Number of predictors: 7
Power: 100 --> 98.7%
Odds ratio: exp(0.07) --> 1.07



Power text: Assuming a linear multiple regression model using a continuous cognition measure as the outcome
variable and seven covariates, a sample size of n=13,000 would allow us to detect a standardized Cohen’s f^2
effect size of 0.001 with 95.1% power at alpha=0.05 for the exposure regression coefficient of a normally
distributed exposure. 

Given the prevalence of cognitive impairment or dementia in the sample is 17.2%, we
have 95.0% power at alpha=0.05 to detect an odds ratio of 1.09 in a logistic regression model for a normally
distributed exposure. Similarly, we have 95.4% power to detect a hazard ratio of 1.09 assuming a normally
distributed exposure that has a correlation of 0.2 with a covariate. (CITATION)

## U01 2023


aim1_power.Rmd - This was CIND/Dementia outcome with regression (GPower 3.1.9.7, https://www.psychologie.hhu.de/arbeitsgruppen/allgemeine-psychologie-und-arbeitspsychologie/gpower.html) and survival analysis, powerSurvEpi R package (Qiu, W., Chavarro, J., Lazarus, R., Rosner, B. & Ma, J. powerSurvEpi: Power and Sample Size Calculation for Survival Analysis of Epidemiological Studies. (2021).)


```{r}
#| label: metals_aim_U01

powerEpiCont.default(n = 13000,
                     theta = 1.09,
                     sigma2 = 1,
                     psi = 0.172,
                     rho2 = 0.2,
                     alpha=0.05)
```

= 95.4% power for the Cox regression model (code based)


Linear multiple regression, GPower (details below), power = 95.1%
Logistic regression, GPower (details below), power = 95.0%, note that this is assuming prevalence of CIND or dementia outcome with 17.2% prevalence of outcome

Power text: Assuming a linear multiple regression model using a continuous cognition measure as the outcome
variable and seven covariates, a sample size of n=13,000 would allow us to detect a standardized Cohen’s f^2
effect size of 0.001 with 95.1% power at alpha=0.05 for the exposure regression coefficient of a normally
distributed exposure. 

Given the prevalence of cognitive impairment or dementia in the sample is 17.2%, we
have 95.0% power at alpha=0.05 to detect an odds ratio of 1.09 in a logistic regression model for a normally
distributed exposure. Similarly, we have 95.4% power to detect a hazard ratio of 1.09 assuming a normally
distributed exposure that has a correlation of 0.2 with a covariate. (CITATION)


aim2_power.Rmd - This was the MWAS (ssizeRNA R package, Bi, R. & Liu, P. ssizeRNA: Sample Size Calculation for RNA-Seq Experimental Design. (2019).)
```{r}
#| label: pfas_pesticides_U01

check.power(m = 2322, 
            nGenes = 707, 
            mu = 1e4, 
            pi0 = 0.90, 
            disp = 0.5, 
            fc = 1.1, 
            sims = 1, 
            fdr = 0.05)
```
power = 92.0%, power unchanged for single metabolite models
Note: m comes from 2322 Dementia or CIND cases, like Aim 1 above
Power text: For untargeted differential abundance metabolomics analysis, assuming that 10% of 707 detected
metabolites are differentially abundant with an average abundance of 10,000 and dispersion of 0.5 among
2,322 individuals with incident CIND or dementia, we have 92.0% power to detect a log-fold-change of 1.1, (q-value false
discovery rate=0.05). (CITATION) 



For modeling direct associations between metabolites and cognitive outcomes,
assuming a linear multiple regression model with continuous cognition measure as the outcome and seven
covariates, a sample size of n=13,000 would allow us to detect a standardized Cohen’s f^2 effect size of 0.001
with  95.0% power (alpha=0.05) for a normally distributed exposure. Given the rate of CIND or dementia in the
sample is 17.2%, we have  95.4% power (alpha=0.05) to detect an odds ratio of 1.09 in a logistic regression.


aim3_power.Rmd - This was the geospatial exposure mixed model with 4 timepoint outcomes, sjstats R package. Looks like this didn't get cited properly in the version I pulled up Bibtex entry:
@Manual{,
    title = {sjstats: Statistical Functions for Regression Models (Version 0.19.0)},
    author = {Daniel Lüdecke},
    year = {2024},
    url = {https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=sjstats},
    doi = {10.5281/zenodo.1284472},
  }
```{r}
#| label: geospatial_u01

set.seed(2016)
samplesize_mixed(
  eff.size = 0.1,
  power = 0.97,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  k = 20000,
  n = 4,
  icc = 0.9
)

set.seed(2016)
samplesize_mixed(
  eff.size = 0.2,
  power = 0.91,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  k = 4000,
  n = 4,
  icc = 0.9
)
```
Power text: With our existing findings of air pollution with ADRD using data through 2016, we expect to have
sufficient power to detect associations with an additional 6 to 8 years of follow-up. For cognitive outcomes, a
final sample size of 22,000 and a conservative intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.9, provides us with 97%
power to identify a small Cohen’s d effect size of 0.1 in a 4 time-point repeated measures linear regression
mixed model for cognitive measures. For the smallest sample of molecular fluid biomarkers, a sample size of
4,018 with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.9 provides us 91% power to identify a small Cohen’s d
effect size of 0.2 in a 4 time-point repeated measures linear mixed model. (CITATION)
Note: this one was the trickiest, never figured how to parameterize it to calculate power from sample size, so had to play with arguments to get our approx. N.
IF you want 13,000 final sample size after 6-8 years of follow-up for bullet 1, then only need 12,925 for 84% power.
